# Macro

`customer_support.obj.macro_management.macro` · v1.0.0 · **draft** · scope **capability**

> A pre-written reply with variables, stored in a library and selected by an agent at the moment of answering. Three things make it an object rather than a string: it carries a claim about how the product behaves, it is sent by a human who may or may not have changed it, and it is reused — so every property it has is multiplied by its volume, including being wrong.
The stored template is not the sent message. The difference between them is the agent's edit, and that difference is the only thing about a macro genuinely worth measuring. A library reported by usage and reviewed by wording is a library nobody has measured.


**The discriminator.** An article is written for the CUSTOMER TO FIND; a macro is written for the AGENT TO SEND — and content that is excellent as one is almost always poor as the other, because an article must survive being read cold by a stranger with no context, while a macro must survive being read immediately after the customer's own words, by someone who has just explained their situation and is checking whether we heard it.


Also called: `Canned Response`, `Saved Reply`, `Quick Text`, `Reply Template`, `Snippet`, `Signature Response`, `Predefined Reply`


### Questions this object answers

- Is there a canned reply that fits this contact, and how much must the agent change before sending it is honest?
- Is this macro still true, or does it describe behaviour the product stopped having?
- Is this macro's volume a support efficiency, or a product defect being financed by support labour?
- Which macros in this library are near-duplicates nobody uses — and which of them is the agent about to pick?
- Did the reply that used this macro end the contact, or start a second one?


### What it is NOT responsible for

- NOT the Knowledge Article. An article is published for a customer to find; a macro is selected by an agent to send. Same answer, opposite readers, and maintaining them as one document produces a macro that reads like documentation or an article that presumes context the reader does not have.

- NOT the Resolution. The macro is the vehicle; the resolution is what made the problem stop. A macro can carry a fix, an apology, a workaround or a stalling message, and nothing on this object can tell you which — Resolution owns that.

- NOT the Conversation. This object is the template in the library, not the message that went out. Conversation owns what was actually said.

- NOT a generated AI answer. A generated reply is composed per contact and governed by what the model was allowed to see; a macro is a fixed artefact somebody approved once. ai_deflection owns the generated case, and conflating them means neither gets the review it needs.

- NOT signatures, greetings or internal note templates. Those carry no claim about the product and therefore cannot be wrong in the way this object is about.

## States

Initial `draft` · terminal `archived`

| State | Means | Entered when | Implies |
|---|---|---|---|
| `draft` | Written, not reviewed. Usually written by an agent mid-shift because the same question came up twice, which is the right reason and the wrong process. | — |  |
| `submitted` | Awaiting review by someone who can check the CLAIM, not the prose. Macro review is almost always a wording review, because wording is the only thing reviewable without outcome data.  | — |  |
| `published` | In the picker and selectable. Reachable by every agent immediately — macros have no staged rollout, which is why a wrong one propagates faster than a wrong article. | — |  |
| `active` | Genuinely in rotation. The only state in which the outcome fields mean anything, because everything else has too little volume to measure. | — | This macro is carrying real queue volume, and any claim it makes is being made to customers at scale today. |
| `dormant` | In the library, effectively unused, and still selectable. The steady state of most macros and the substance of sprawl. Nothing is broken, nobody is harmed, and the picker gets slightly worse for everyone.  | — |  |
| `at_risk` | Something concrete says it is now wrong — a release in its product area, the fix of the issue it describes, or an outcome profile that turned. Never entered from age alone; a policy macro can be correct for years.  | `exists: commitment.due_at` AND `days_since(commitment.due_at) > 30` |  |
| `superseded` | A newer macro carries the answer and both are still in the picker. The dangerous window, and in practice a permanent one — supersession is recorded and retirement is not, so the old macro keeps being chosen by whoever searched a word it happens to contain.  | — |  |
| `archived` | Removed from the picker. The rarest transition in this object's lifecycle, and the one that would fix most of what is wrong with macro libraries. | — |  |

## Preconditions

- **`macro.intent_must_be_classified_first`** A macro may not be selected before the contact's intent has been resolved. Selecting against title keywords instead is not a weaker version of the same act — it is a different act, and it is the mechanism that produces the wrong-question send.
 _(unmet → block)_
- **`macro.customers_own_words_must_be_available`** The customer's actual message must be resolvable, not just its classification. Intent says what kind of question it is; only the message says whether this particular person has already tried the thing the macro is about to tell them to try.
 _(unmet → degrade)_
- **`macro.entitlement_required_when_the_body_promises`** A macro whose body contains a response time, a remedy or a refund term may not be sent until entitlement is resolved. The promise is real the moment it is sent, and it was written months ago by someone who did not know who would receive it.
 _(unmet → block)_
- **`macro.linked_article_must_resolve`** If the macro links an article, the article must be resolvable and reachable by THIS requester. Degrade rather than block: sending the answer without the link is worse than sending it with a link, and both are better than sending a link to a page the customer cannot open.
 _(unmet → degrade)_
- **`macro.locale_must_match_the_requester`** A macro in a locale the requester does not read is not a faster reply, it is a second contact with a translation problem attached. _(unmet → block)_
- **`macro.no_macro_selection_while_they_owe_us`** When the observed ball is in the customer's court there is nothing to answer, and any macro selected in that state is a chase or a close — both of which are different acts with different rules.
 _(unmet → degrade)_


## Constraints

- **`macro.body_promise_may_not_exceed_entitlement`** No macro containing a response-time or remedy promise may be sent to an account whose entitlement does not cover it.
- **`macro.agent_only_never_reaches_a_customer`** A macro with audience_scope = agent_only may not be sent on a customer-facing channel.
- **`macro.no_customer_identifiers_in_the_body`** A macro drafted from a real case may not carry the originating account's name, hostname, ticket text or reproduction data.
- **`macro.locale_variant_verified_separately`** A translated macro does not inherit the source macro's verification. It carries its own, or it is unverified. _(soft)_
- **`macro.no_macro_as_the_substantive_reply_on_an_escalation`** Once a thread is escalated, a macro may not be the substantive reply.
- **`macro.completion_tokens_must_be_resolved_before_send`** A sent message may not contain an unresolved placeholder token.
- **`macro.no_auto_send_without_resolved_intent`** A macro may not be sent automatically on inferred intent alone, at any confidence.


## Business rules

- **`macro.every_customer_facing_macro_has_a_required_edit`** A customer-facing macro of type `answer` must carry at least one variable the agent cannot leave empty. A macro that can be sent with zero thought will be, on the busiest day, to the customer who can least afford it.
 — _Warning rather than blocking because the exceptions are real — incident notices and regulated statements are complete on purpose. But the default must lean the other way, because every other force in the system pushes toward complete macros and nothing pushes back.
_
- **`macro.high_share_is_raised_before_it_is_rewritten`** A macro above a small share of its queue must be raised as a product or content finding before any wording change is made to it. The rewrite is the consolation prize, not the response.
 — _Rewriting is available to the support team this afternoon; filing the product fix is somebody else's roadmap and a six-month argument. The local move is always available and always feels productive, which is exactly why the rule has to exist.
_
- **`macro.supersede_requires_retirement`** Publishing a replacement must retire the predecessor from the picker in the same action. Marking it superseded while leaving it selectable is not retirement. — _The single mechanism of sprawl. Every library that grew to four hundred macros did it one un-retired predecessor at a time, and each one was individually defensible._
- **`macro.issue_fix_invalidates_the_macro`** When the issue a macro documents is resolved, the macro moves to at_risk immediately and may not be sent until re-verified. — _Otherwise we walk customers through workarounds for bugs we already fixed. This is the confidently-wrong reply, which costs more than the slow one, and it is the failure mode macros produce that articles largely do not.
_
- **`macro.a_promise_inside_a_macro_is_still_a_commitment`** A macro body containing a time-bound promise must create a tracked commitment on send. A macro that promises and records nothing is the cheapest way there is to manufacture broken promises at scale.
 — _Customers forgive slow far more readily than they forgive silence after a specific date was given — and the date in a macro was given by a template, so nobody feels personally responsible for it. Half of every library says "within 24 hours" and almost none of it creates a clock.
_
- **`macro.must_not_contradict_its_linked_article`** A macro whose claims contradict the article it links may not be sent until one of them is corrected. — _The customer can read both. Enterprise customers routinely do, because they forward our replies internally and then check the docs._
- **`macro.closing_macros_may_not_claim_resolution`** A macro of type `closing` sent after customer silence must state that we are closing for lack of response and must invite a reply. It may not assert that the problem was resolved.
 — _Auto-close macros that claim resolution move an abandonment out of the queue metrics and into the churn metrics, where support is not measured. The queue looks healthier and the company is not.
_
- **`macro.maintenance_promise_overdue_flags_before_reuse`** A macro with an overdue promised fix must be flagged to the agent before it is sent again.


## Exceptions — where the rules above are legitimately wrong

- **During a declared major incident, sending the identical unedited message to four hundred customers is correct.
** — When the fact is the same for everyone, consistency IS the personalisation. Four hundred individually-worded versions of the same outage produce four hundred slightly different accounts of what happened, which customers compare on social media within the hour. The incident object exists precisely to make this the default, and an agent editing an incident notice to sound warmer is committing the error, not avoiding it.
 _(overrides macro.every_customer_facing_macro_has_a_required_edit, macro.no_macro_as_the_substantive_reply_on_an_escalation, macro.sent_without_a_single_edit)_
- **Refund terms, privacy responses, security disclosures and legally reviewed statements are complete macros by design, and editing them is the defect.
** — The wording was approved as a whole by someone who is accountable for it. An agent improving the tone of a data-deletion confirmation has changed a legal statement. The correct shape here is a complete, locked body with a personal sentence ABOVE it, not a body with blanks in it.
 _(overrides macro.every_customer_facing_macro_has_a_required_edit)_
- **An agent answering in a language they do not write fluently should use MORE complete macros, not fewer.
** — The usual argument runs one way — personalise more — and it is wrong here. A partial macro completed in halting phrasing reads as less competent than a complete one used well, and the customer attributes the awkwardness to the company rather than to a second-language speaker doing something difficult. The right fix is a properly localised complete macro plus a personal opening line the agent can manage.

- **A first-response acknowledgement may be entirely canned, provided it is unmistakably an acknowledgement and a substantive reply follows.** — The failure is never that the acknowledgement was templated — it is passing a template off as an answer. An honest "we have this, a human is looking, here is the reference" is useful precisely because it makes no claim. What it must never do is stop a first-response clock while pretending to have answered something.
 _(overrides macro.no_auto_send_without_resolved_intent)_
- **A macro carrying an unusually large share of a queue during a known migration, pricing change or seasonal window is correct and temporary.
** — Raising it as a product finding wastes the finding and trains whoever receives it to ignore the next one. The discriminator is whether the share is DECLINING on its own — a spike resolves without intervention, a gap does not — which needs a time series nobody currently keeps, so the judgement stays human for now.
 _(overrides macro.high_share_is_raised_before_it_is_rewritten, macro.carrying_an_outsized_share_of_a_queue)_
- **Some requesters explicitly want the standard text — procurement, security questionnaires, compliance contacts forwarding our answer to a third party.
** — Personalising a security-posture reply for someone whose actual job is to paste it into a vendor assessment makes their job harder and ours slower. The tell is a requester who asks in formal, reusable language and never reacts to tone. Read the request, not the policy.



## Best practices

- **Every customer-facing answer macro carries at least one blank the agent cannot leave empty.** — It is the only structural defence against the unedited send. Policy and training are not defences — they are asks made of the person under the most time pressure in the company.

- **The opening sentence names this customer's specific situation and is written fresh every time. Everything below it may be templated.** — Customers decide whether they were heard in the first sentence and then read the rest with that verdict already made. This buys most of the benefit of personalisation for a fraction of the cost, which is why it survives contact with a busy queue.

- **Title macros in the customer's words — the question they asked — not in ours, the answer we give.** — Agents search the picker under pressure. A library indexed by our answers means the search that finds a macro is a search for our vocabulary, and the wrong-question send becomes a property of the library rather than a mistake by a person.

- **Publishing a macro requires retiring one. The library has a cap and the cap is enforced.** — Nothing else stops sprawl, because every individual addition is justified and every individual retirement is contested. A cap converts an unwinnable argument about each macro into a decidable comparison between two.

- **Macro reviews look at follow-up rate, reopen rate and escalation rate. Wording is reviewed only for macros the outcomes have already flagged.** — Wording reviews are cheap, satisfying, infinitely repeatable and uncorrelated with anything. A team can rewrite a library twice a year and change no customer's experience at all.

- **A macro points at the article rather than duplicating its content.** — One maintained copy instead of two that diverge. When both exist the macro is corrected first and the public article silently becomes the wrong one.
- **Macros of type known_issue and workaround are created with an expiry date and disappear from the picker on it.** — A review date requires somebody to act for the macro to stop; an expiry requires somebody to act for it to continue. Given that nobody acts, the two defaults produce opposite outcomes, and only one of them is safe.

- **Report library size, dormant share and near-duplicate share alongside any macro-level number.** — Every macro can look reasonable while the library is unusable. The thing agents actually experience is the picker, and no per-macro metric describes it.



## Anti-patterns

- **A macro is chosen because a word in its title matched a word in the customer's message, and it answers something they did not ask.** — tempting because The picker is searched by keyword under queue pressure, with the customer's message still on screen. One word matches, the match feels like a decision, and selecting is indistinguishable from deciding when both take the same two seconds. Nothing in the tool marks the difference.
 Instead: Select against classified intent, never against title keywords; title macros by the customer's question; make the first sentence non-canned so the mismatch is caught while writing it.

- **Over time every macro in the library becomes sendable with zero edits.** — tempting because Complete macros are measurably faster and handle time is measured. Whoever writes a skeleton is optimising unedited_send_rate, which nobody reports; whoever completes a skeleton is optimising handle time, which everyone reports. The drift needs no advocate — it happens through ordinary editing by people doing their jobs well.
 Instead: Mandatory variables enforced by the tool; report unedited_send_rate beside handle time or do not report handle time.
- **A macro carrying a third of a queue gets a wording rewrite, three times, over a year.** — tempting because Rewriting is a decision the support team can make alone this afternoon. Filing the product fix is somebody else's roadmap and a six-month argument that support usually loses. The local move is always available, always feels productive, and produces a visible artefact.
 Instead: Raise the volume as a product or content finding first. The rewrite is the consolation prize.
- **The library grows monotonically until agents are searching four versions of the same refund reply.** — tempting because Adding is free and visibly helpful; deleting can break somebody's workflow and is visibly a loss. No one owns the library as a whole, so every local decision is correct and the aggregate is a picker nobody can search. Supersession is recorded; retirement is not.
 Instead: A named library owner, one-in-one-out, retirement enforced on supersede, and near-duplicate share reported monthly.
- **A workaround macro is still being sent months after the bug it works around was fixed.** — tempting because Macros sit outside every documentation review that exists. They have no owner, no review cycle and no reader — unlike an article, nobody ever reads a macro as a customer would. It fails only inside one live reply, one customer at a time, which is the slowest possible way to discover anything.
 Instead: Expiry dates on known-issue and workaround macros; wire the issue-fixed event to every macro on that edge.
- **Macro usage is presented as an efficiency metric, and rising usage as a maturing team.** — tempting because Usage is the only macro number that is free to collect, and it goes up. It makes a good slide, it flatters the team, and no one has to argue with it because the alternative numbers do not exist.
 Instead: Publish usage only joined to reopen and follow-up rates on the same replies. An unjoined usage number should not leave the team that produced it.
- **The same answer is kept in a macro and in an article, and they diverge.** — tempting because The macro is edited in the moment by whoever noticed the problem; the article needs a review cycle and an owner who may have left. So the macro becomes right first and the article rots while looking maintained, and the divergence is always in the same direction.
 Instead: The macro links the article rather than restating it. One copy, one owner, one verification date.
- **"We haven't heard back, so we're closing this" is sent at volume and counted as resolved work.** — tempting because It converts an aging ticket into a resolved one with a single click, it is defensible in every individual case, and the alternative — chasing properly and holding the ticket open — makes every duration metric on the queue look worse.
 Instead: One genuine chase before any close; a closing macro that explicitly invites a reply and never asserts the problem was resolved.

## Inputs

- **knowledge_base** — the macro library — body, title, variables, locale, owner
- **ticket** — which macro was applied, and how much of it was changed
- **email** — whether we replied, and whether they came straight back
- **email** — when the customer last wrote
- **derived** — observation balance across the thread
- **manual_entry** — a promised macro fix and its date
- **manual_entry** — what the promised fix was
- **survey** — satisfaction on interactions where a macro was sent
- **telemetry** — releases in the product area this macro describes
- **help_center** — the article this macro should mirror
- **chat** — macros sent in live conversation, where the pressure to send unedited is highest


## Outputs

- **`fit_confidence_bp`** How well this macro matches the contact in front of us. Low confidence must route to writing, not to the next-best macro. → L4.decision_maker, L5.communication_planning
- **`requires_agent_completion`** Whether the agent must write something before this can go out. The single most useful boolean this object produces, and the one a send button should be wired to.
 → L5.communication_planning, L5.2.channel_planner
- **`send_ready`** Whether this may be sent right now at all. False on an overdue maintenance promise, a post-verification release, or an escalated thread. → L5.communication_planning, L5.2.channel_planner
- **`product_gap_signal`** The finding hidden inside this macro's volume. Emitted so it reaches the product backlog rather than the wording queue, which is where it currently goes.
 → L4.reasoning_unit, L6.learning_unit
- **`content_gap_signal`** Demand this macro is absorbing that an article should be answering without a human at all. → L4.reasoning_unit
- **`retirement_candidate`** Whether this macro should leave the picker. The output nobody acts on, which is why every library grows monotonically. → L5.execution_planning
- **`library_health_contribution`** This macro's contribution to how hard the picker is to search. Only meaningful in aggregate, and the aggregate is the thing worth managing. → L6.learning_unit


## Events

- **`macro.published`** Macro Published
- **`macro.sent_unedited`** Macro Sent Unedited
- **`macro.answered_and_bounced`** Reply Answered And Bounced
- **`macro.rewrite_promise_missed`** Promised Macro Fix Missed
- **`macro.orphaned`** Macro Orphaned
- **`macro.contradicted_by_a_fix`** Contradicted By A Fix — invalidates last_verified_at, verified_against_version, maintenance_state, body
- **`macro.superseded_without_retirement`** Superseded Without Retirement
- **`macro.share_crossed_the_finding_line`** Macro Share Crossed The Finding Line


## Actions

- **Select a macro against the classified intent** (agent) — Narrows the picker to macros that claim this intent. The alternative — searching titles by keyword — is the wrong-question failure in its raw form.
- **Complete the required variables** (agent) — The step this entire object exists to protect. It costs seconds and is the whole difference between a fast reply and a message proving nobody read theirs.
- **Rewrite the first sentence in the customer's own terms** (agent) — The cheapest available defence. A customer decides whether they were heard in the first sentence; everything after it can be canned without being detected.

- **Send the completed reply** (agent) — Irreversible and multiplied by volume. Every property of the template becomes a property of a relationship at this moment.
- **Convert a complete macro into a partial one** (human) — The highest-yield and least popular fix in the library, because it deliberately makes agents slower on a number they are measured on in order to improve one nobody reports. Expect it to be resisted for entirely rational reasons.

- **Replace restated content with a link to the article** (agent) — Collapses two maintained copies into one. When they are maintained separately the macro wins and the public article rots.
- **Merge near-duplicates into one macro with a variable** (human) — Merge rather than delete. The differences between duplicates are usually a plan or a region, which is a variable, not a separate macro.
- **Retire the macro and point its users at the survivor** (human) — The action that would fix most of what is wrong with macro libraries and is almost never taken, because retiring visibly removes something and adding visibly gives something.
- **Raise the macro's volume as a product or content finding** (human) — Moves the cost from the support line to the line that owns it. Slower and less satisfying than a rewrite, and the only one of the two that ever makes the macro unnecessary.

- **Re-verify the macro's claim against the shipping product** (human) — Sets last_verified_at AND verified_against_version. Either alone is theatre — a date with no referent is not a verification.
- **Write a new macro only on the second occurrence** (agent) — Drafting from one case produces a macro about one customer. The second occurrence is what proves the question is general, and it is also the gate that keeps the library from growing on enthusiasm.



## Evidence

- **ticket** · 9000 bp — The helpdesk record of which macro was applied and what was changed before sending. The receipt this object needs, the receipt no support brain currently has, and the reason nine of thirteen patterns here cannot fire.

- **telemetry** · 8000 bp — Release and version data for the surface the macro makes claims about. The only source that can prove a macro wrong rather than merely old.
- **email** · 7500 bp — The reply as actually sent, and the only place the edited body survives outside the helpdesk. Strong, timestamped, and the only source the pipeline actually reads today.

- **chat** · 6500 bp — Where the unedited send is most likely and least observed. Not ingested, so its absence quietly biases every measurement here toward the more careful channel.
- **survey** · 5500 bp — The customer's verdict on a reply. Confounded by which contacts receive macros at all, so it is only readable within an intent.
- **knowledge_base** · 5000 bp — The macro library itself. Proves the template exists and says nothing about what was sent — the source most often mistaken for proof.
- **help_center** · 4000 bp — The published article this macro should mirror. Establishes what the customer-facing claim is, so divergence becomes visible.
- **derived** · 3500 bp — Graph degree and thread sentiment. Corroborating only — it reorders a review queue and decides nothing.
- **manual_entry** · 2500 bp — An agent's note or a promised fix. Honest, unverifiable, and written by the person who would have to do the work.


## Metrics

- **unedited_send_rate** (percent) — Share of sends where not one character changed. The number this object exists to produce, computable by any helpdesk from two strings it already stores, and reported by none of them.

- **macro_share_of_replies** (percent) — Share of a queue's replies running through one macro. A target band and not a maximum: too low means the library is unusable and agents are retyping the same answer, too high means a gap is being financed by labour.

- **macro_to_followup_rate** (percent) — Sends followed by another message from the same customer on the same intent. The wrong-question rate.
- **macro_reopen_rate** (percent) — Reopens on tickets a macro resolved, against the queue's own norm. Harder to game than any survey, because the customer has to act.
- **near_duplicate_share** (percent) — Share of the library with a close counterpart. The sprawl number, computable from the bodies today, computed nowhere.
- **dormant_macro_share** (percent) — Share of published macros not sent in the last quarter. Rises monotonically in every organisation because the retirement action exists and is never taken.

- **median_days_since_verification** (days) — Use the median, never the mean. A handful of hot macros edited weekly hides a long tail nobody has checked since the product looked different.

- **escalation_rate_after_macro** (percent) — Sends shortly followed by an escalation request. Small numbers here matter more than large numbers anywhere else on this object.

## Examples

- **Password reset macro, one required variable, sent 400 times a month, reopen rate at the queue norm** _(typical)_ — A macro working exactly as intended. High volume here is not a product finding — the task is genuinely repetitive and self-service already covers it for those who look. This is the case that makes the blanket rule "high share means a product gap" wrong, and why queue_share is a context factor rather than an increasing one.

- **Refund policy macro sent to a customer asking why their approved refund had not arrived** _(misclassification)_ — The canonical wrong-question send. The word "refund" matched, the macro was accurate, well-written and recently verified, and it explained the policy to someone who had already read it and was asking about a payment. The customer's next message was to cancel. Nothing on this object other than the intent ref could have prevented it.

- **Identical outage notice sent unedited to 400 customers during a declared major incident** _(edge)_ — Correct, and it violates the object's headline practice. Consistency is the personalisation when the fact is the same for everyone — see the major-incident exception. An agent warming up the wording here is committing the error, not avoiding it.

- **Billing macro rewritten four times in a year while the invoice bug it explains stayed open** _(counterexample)_ — Every rewrite made the macro clearer and none of them reduced the volume by anything. The macro's excellence became the reason the gap survived: the problem was being handled, so it was not a problem. The finding was available from month one in the share number nobody looked at.

- **Four refund macros in the picker; three last used eleven months ago, all still selectable** _(edge)_ — Sprawl in its normal state. Nothing is broken and nobody is harmed until an agent in a hurry picks the 2023 one with the old policy in it. The duplicates also split the volume four ways, which is why none of them ever looked significant enough to review.

- **Known-issue workaround macro still in rotation two releases after the fix shipped** _(misclassification)_ — We told customers, confidently and in writing, to do something that no longer works, for a problem that no longer exists. Discovered by a customer. This is the failure macros produce that articles largely do not, because an article is at least read by strangers who can notice.

- **"We haven't heard back so we're closing this" — 900 sends a quarter, reopen rate four times the queue norm** _(counterexample)_ — The highest-volume macro in many libraries and the least examined, because it is classified as hygiene rather than as an answer. It is the single clearest case for separating macro_type = closing from macro_type = answer.

- **Onboarding macro promising a callback within 24 hours, sent 200 times, creating no commitment record** _(edge)_ — A promise made two hundred times by a template that nobody feels personally responsible for. Half of every library contains a sentence like this and almost none of it starts a clock. Customers forgive slow; they do not forgive a named commitment followed by silence.


## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional** · completeness **partial**


> SCOPED rather than core, and the argument is the reference graph rather than taste. A macro is an artefact of how ONE TEAM ANSWERS. Triage decides what a thing is before any reply exists and has no use for a reply template; incident response composes its message once, deliberately, through the incident object; capacity planning counts contacts and is indifferent to their phrasing. Exactly one capability — macro_management — loads it, so objects/core/ would be wrong in the mechanical sense the domain enforces, and wrong in a second sense too: an object in the load-set is a suggestion, and suggesting a reply template to a capability whose correct behaviour is to write from scratch is an active harm rather than harmless noise.
Thirteen patterns: FIVE executable, EIGHT needs_signal. Not one of the five can see that a macro was sent. They read a maintenance commitment, graph degree twice, the shape of a reply round-trip, and thread sentiment — the only things in today's substrate that touch this object at all. Every one is scored between 4000 and 7500 and every one carries a named false_positive, because the honest description of all five is "aggregate prior", not "finding". macro.no_trace_anywhere_in_the_graph is the most compromised of them and is kept anyway, because sprawl is the second-largest thing wrong with macro libraries and this is the only executable handle on it that exists; it should be DELETED, not promoted, on the day macro.use_count_30d lands.
The eight needs_signal entries are ranked by what they unlock, and the first two are not close. macro_applied joined to macro.edit_distance_at_send is the whole object: both strings are stored by every helpdesk on the market, the subtraction is trivial, and the result is the difference between a library reviewable only by wording and one reviewable by whether anybody thought before sending. Second is macro.use_count_30d over ticket.queue, because that is what turns a support efficiency story into a product bill. Everything else here is downstream of those two.
Signal names proposed by this object and not yet in vocabulary planned_substrate: macro_applied (obs_kind), macro.macro_ref, macro.edit_distance_at_send, macro.use_count_30d, macro.body_text, knowledge.body_text, derived.macro_similarity. product.released_at, product.surface_version and knowledge.body_text overlap with asks already made by knowledge_article — one emitter serves both, and they should be counted once in the backlog rather than twice.
One executable pattern was considered and deliberately NOT authored: `has_obs: followup_sent` alone, as a proxy for "a macro was sent". It is grammatical, it would have put the object's headline metric under a green tick, and it measures outbound email. That is structurally identical to binding "SLA breach imminent" to unanswered_email, which the domain header names as the failure this architecture exists to prevent.
anti_patterns is the longest section here on purpose. Macros fail in ways that are individually rational — every why_it_happens describes a decision a competent person makes for good reasons — so a system that treats these as carelessness will be ignored by the people it is advising. exceptions matters for the mirror reason: five of the six are cases where "always personalise" is actively wrong, and an assistant that does not know them will be dismissed by a support lead inside a day.
